RE: Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P) 
 
Dear Secretary Oz: 
 
The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation thanks the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) for the 
opportunity to respond to the Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed 
rule and Requests for Information (RFIs).  
 
Cystic fibrosis is a life-threatening genetic disease that causes the body to produce thick, sticky mucus 
that clogs the lungs and digestive system which can lead to life-threatening infections. As a complex, 
multi-system condition, CF requires targeted, specialized treatment and medications. Through careful, 
aggressive, and continuously improving disease management, the average life expectancy for people 
with cystic fibrosis has risen steadily over the last few decades. This milestone reflects over 50 years of 
hard work to improve CF treatments, develop evidence-based standards of care, and encourage 
adherence to a lifetime of chronic care. However, this system of care and the improvements in length 
and quality of life can only be realized if people with CF have access to essential therapies.  
 
Prior authorization is a time-consuming process that can burden providers, divert valuable resources 
away from direct patient care, and cause delays in patient access to needed treatment. This process is 
particularly burdensome for the CF community as people with CF must adhere to intensive, ongoing 
treatment plans in order to stay healthy. Prior authorization policies also present a unique set of 
challenges for people with CF and other lifelong, chronic diseases. For CF patients, their diagnosis will 
never change; they will take many of the same drugs throughout their lifetime and it is unnecessary to 
require providers to continuously request reauthorizations and provide duplicative information in order 
to demonstrate the medical necessity of these therapies. 
 
In response to the Proposed Rule and the questions in the RFIs, the CF Foundation provides the 
following comments.

Application Programming Interface (APIs) 
 
Patient Access API 
The CF Foundation supports increased transparency for patients through a standardized system across 
different payer types and coverage programs. This transparency will allow patients to quickly access 
prior authorization decisions for drugs and has the potential to limit delays or gaps in accessing needed 
treatments for people with CF covered under these plans. 
 
Specifically, increased interoperability between systems for drugs has the potential to benefit patients, 
like people with CF, by easing administrative burdens and reducing the risk of delays or gaps in 
treatments. For instance, people with CF often need to deal with higher levels of paperwork than the 
average beneficiary and can experience interruptions in care when they change insurance and need new 
prior authorization for their treatments.1 Having information available in the Payer-to-Payer APIs such as 
previously approved prior authorizations after a patient switches payers would support continuity of 
care in these instances. For people with CF, these policies can help maintain health and quality of life 
through consistent access to therapies, and avoid complications that can cause infections or irreversible 
lung damage.  
 
Providing patients with real-time prescription drug cost and coverage information through the Patient 
Access API is also critical. Access to this information would allow patients to better track the status of 
prior authorization decisions and anticipated out-of-pocket costs. In nearly 19 percent of all prior 
authorization-related cases reported to the Foundation in the last 5 years, patients were unaware that 
the prior authorization was not submitted.2 Lack of visibility into the process contributes to confusion 
and unexpected costs and the Foundation appreciates efforts to improve transparency.  
 
To ensure these tools are accessible and effective, CMS should establish clear standards for usability and 
equity. Patient-facing interfaces should use plain language and meet the needs of individuals with 
disabilities and limited English proficiency, consistent with the Department of Justiceâ€™s recommended 
strategies for developing multilingual digital services. This platform should indicate when important 
information, like disclaimers, are not translated online and direct people to appropriate resources. in 
addition, any telephonic consumer assistance should offer non-English voicemail menus, and customer 
service representatives should have access to qualified interpreters. Finally, CMS should account for 
individuals who have limited digital or broadband access that may not be able to use this digital platform 
to obtain this information electronically. It is imperative that there is equitable access to the necessary 
coverage information for all people covered under these plans. 
 
Provider Adoption and Use of APIs 
To maximize the impact of interoperability requirements, CMS should prioritize strategies to accelerate 
provider adoption of APIs and electronic prior authorization tools. Recent data demonstrates significant 
gaps in provider readiness, with one national survey finding that one third of providers had not begun 
implementation of required APIs and nearly two-thirds were unsure of their progress, citing barriers

such as cost, technical complexity, and challenges coordinating with vendors and health plans.3 CMS 
should explore targeted technical assistance, pilot programs, and incentives to support adoption.   
 
Additionally, CMS should require the collection and public reporting of API usage metrics, including 
utilization rates by provider type, plan, and geographic region. These data will be critical to identifying 
gaps in adoption and ensuring that interoperability investments translate into meaningful improvements 
in patient access. 
 
Improving Prior Authorization Processes 
We strongly support CMSâ€™s proposal to extend electronic prior authorization requirements to 
prescription drugs across both medical and pharmacy benefits. However, inclusion of drugs in electronic 
workflows alone will not resolve longstanding access barriers. CMS should pair these requirements with 
substantive policy reforms, including ensuring continuity of care through detailed denial explanations, 
further shortening of decision timelines where possible, and eliminating unnecessary repeat 
reauthorizations.  
 
The CF Foundation supports the proposed requirement for payers to provide a specific reason when a 
prior authorization is denied but urges CMS to further strengthen these requirements. To ensure these 
requirements meaningfully improve transparency, CMS should require plans to provide detailed and 
actionable denial explanations. At minimum, denial notices should include the specific clinical criteria or 
coverage policy used to make the determination, clearly identifying any missing documentation, and 
outline precise next steps for resubmission or appeal. Explanations that rely on broad or non-specific 
language, such as â€œfailure to establish medical necessity,â€ do not provide sufficient information for 
providers or patients to respond effectively and should not be permitted. 
 
Furthermore, we support CMSâ€™s proposal to require impacted payers to send prior authorization 
decisions for drugs within 72 hours for standard requests and 24 hours for expedited requests and we 
strongly encourage the agency to further shorten timelines where feasible, including considering a 24-
hour standard for all drug prior authorization decisions. Prior authorizations should be promptly 
reviewed with the decision shared in a transparent manner to both the provider and the patient, so they 
are not the cause of delayed treatment. In 2023, 56% of callers to the CF Foundationâ€™s Compass program 
with prior authorization or payer formulary issues experienced a delay in care. Because CF is a 
progressive disease, patients who delay or forgo treatment â€“ even for as little as a few days â€“ face 
increased risk of lung exacerbations, costly hospitalizations, and potentially irreversible lung damage. 
CMS should also limit the use of timeframe extensions, require timely notification to patients and 
providers when extensions are applied, and ensure that any delays are clearly justified. Strengthening 
and enforcing these timelines will be critical to reducing barriers to timely treatment.  
 
CMS should also address the growing use of alternative funding programs (AFPs) and similar third party 
programs that operate outside the traditional benefit design and attempt to circumvent prior 
authorization safeguards and undermine established patient protections. Some of these programs place 
patients in a prior authorization standstill by carving out a covered benefit and refusing to issue a clear 
coverage determination unless the patient agrees to enroll in the AFP. Rather than processing the 
request through standard prior authorization channels, plans delay or withhold decisions, leaving

patients and providers without clarity on approval status or next steps. As a result, patients are denied 
access to procedural protections CMS seeks to strengthen in this proposed rule, including detailed and 
actionable denial notices and meaningful opportunities to request reconsideration or file an appeal. 
CMS has emphasized that denial determinations must provide sufficient detail to enable patients and 
providers to take action and that beneficiaries must have timely access to appeal pathways.  AFPs 
circumvent these protections by preventing a formal determination altogether, effectively denying 
patients their right to appeal. CMS should therefore clarify that any utilization management or 
coverage-related requirements, including those implemented through AFPs, must comply with prior 
authorization standards, including requirements for specific denial explanations, clear instructions for 
reconsideration and appeal, and enforceable timelines that preserve patientsâ€™ ability to seek timely 
review. 
 
Finally, we urge CMS to establish clear protections that reduce unnecessary repeat prior authorizations 
for patients with chronic conditions requiring long-term or lifelong therapies, including by adopting 
extended approval timeframes and exploring â€œgold cardingâ€ to automatically approve prior 
authorizations for providers with a demonstrated history of prior authorization approvals. Currently, 
individuals with cystic fibrosis remain on many therapies indefinitely, and these medications have well-
defined indications that limit use to appropriate patients. Requiring repeated reauthorization for stable, 
long-term treatments provides little clinical value while imposing significant administrative burden on 
both providers and patients. CMS should require that prior authorization approvals remain valid for the 
duration of treatment or for extended clinically appropriate periods and take steps to streamline 
approvals for high-performing providers. These policies would reduce unnecessary burden, improve 
continuity of care, and allow care teams to focus on delivering high-quality clinical care rather than 
administrative processes. 
 
Public Reporting  
We support CMSâ€™s efforts to expand reporting on prior authorization activity and outcomes, and urge 
the agency to adopt additional measures to improve transparency and accountability. CMS should 
require reporting of total prior authorization requests, approvals, denials, appeals, and use of extended 
timeframes across both standard and expedited requests.  
 
To better understand the impact on patients, CMS should require data to be disaggregated by factors 
such as condition, service type, geographic region, and patient demographics. CMS should also 
standardize reporting formats and require that this information be made publicly available on a regular 
basis. Increased transparency will enable patients, researchers, and policymakers to identify disparities 
in access and hold plans accountable for prior authorization practices. 
 
Request for Information: Step Therapy 
In addition to burdensome prior authorization, step therapy presents a significant barrier to timely and 
appropriate care for people with CF. For some people with CF, the first-line modulator therapy may not 
be clinically appropriate. For example, Trikafta (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor) can have tolerability 
issues or adverse side effects that necessitate discontinuation.4 In these cases, switching to an 
alternative therapy may be the most effective course of treatment; however, step therapy requirements 
can force patients to retry previously ineffective or intolerable therapies and impose unnecessary 
clinical risk.  
 
4Pasley K, Eisner M, Sliemers S, Young R, Dell ML, McCoy KS, May A. Mental Health of Pediatric Patients with Cystic 
Fibrosis after 18 Months on Elexacaftor-Tezacaftor-Ivacaftor Therapy. Pediatric Pulmonology, 2025;60:e27393  
5

4550 Montgomery Avenue, Suite 1100N, Bethesda, Maryland 20814 
 
301.951.4422     800.FIGHT.CF     Fax: 301.951.6378 
www.cff.org     email: info@cff.org 
 
Step therapy can also disrupt care for people with CF who are stable on an existing regimen. Requiring 
these individuals to revert to a different therapy solely to satisfy step therapy protocols can lead to 
treatment instability and avoidable health consequences. These challenges are further exacerbated 
when patients transition between payers that do not adequately account for prior step therapy 
completion or previous authorization determinations. CMS should ensure that plans honor prior step 
therapy history and leverage interoperability tools, including payer-to-payer APIs, to facilitate continuity 
of care. Sharing step therapy and prior authorization data across plans will be critical to preventing 
unnecessary and harmful treatment disruptions.  
 
Request for Information: Laboratory Test and Durable Medical Equipment, Prosthetics, Orthotics, and 
Supplies Items 
Prior authorizations on durable medical equipment (DME) are also burdensome to patients and 
providers and can create access issues. People with CF often have to use DME as part of their treatment, 
including occasionally being required to use supplemental oxygen. Although there are several different 
types of supplemental oxygen, liquid oxygen is the most lightweight and portable. Concentrators for 
other types of oxygen can be bulky, heavy, and not provide the same high flow rate as liquid oxygen, 
preventing patients from doing daily activities. Access to liquid oxygen can provide a level of 
independence and benefit to people with CF that other forms of oxygen cannot. However, due to prior 
authorization requirements, it is often unavailable to patients. Prior authorization delays or denials for 
liquid oxygen create barriers that prevent patients from participating in activities such as work, family 
engagements, and more. We encourage CMS to explore ways to reduce unnecessary prior 
authorizations on these items.  
  
************* 
 
The CF Foundation appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed rule and RFIs. We 
look forward to working with CMS on these critical issues to ensure access and affordability for people 
with CF. 
 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
Mary B. Dwight 
Senior Vice President 
Chief Policy and Advocacy Officer

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Cystic Fibrosis Foundation; signed by Mary B. Dwight, Senior Vice President and Chief Policy and Advocacy Officer.
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** The organization represents people with cystic fibrosis and cites CF Foundation Compass case management data, WEDI survey results, and clinical literature on cystic fibrosis therapies.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation strongly supports extending electronic prior authorization requirements to prescription drugs across medical and pharmacy benefits, emphasizing that delays and repeated reauthorizations can seriously harm people with lifelong chronic diseases. It recommends more actionable denial explanations, shorter and enforceable drug PA timelines, API usability and equity safeguards, public API usage reporting, protections against alternative funding programs, reduced repeat prior authorizations for chronic therapies, and use of payer-to-payer APIs to preserve prior authorization and step therapy history.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; PATIENT ACCESS API / PAYER-TO-PAYER API under GENERAL; GENERAL RFIs on step therapy and lab/DME.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No CFR citations. The comment references CMS-0062-P and CMS interoperability/prior authorization requirements generally.
- **Standards referenced:** APIs; Patient Access API; Payer-to-Payer APIs; electronic prior authorization tools; no named FHIR IGs or NCPDP standards discussed in detail.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Patient Access API and Payer-to-Payer Continuity**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** The Foundation states that standardized digital access to prior authorization decisions, previously approved prior authorizations, and real-time drug cost/coverage information can reduce care disruptions when patients change insurance.
- **Specific request:** CMS should ensure prior authorization status, previous approvals, and drug cost/coverage information are accessible through patient and payer-to-payer APIs in ways that support continuity of care.

**Topic 2: Usability and Equity in Patient-Facing Interfaces**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Digital tools may not benefit all patients unless they are accessible to people with disabilities, limited English proficiency, and limited broadband or digital access.
- **Specific request:** CMS should establish plain-language, multilingual, disability-accessible, and non-digital assistance standards, including translated disclaimers, interpreter access, and accommodation for people without reliable digital access.

**Topic 3: Provider Adoption and API Usage Metrics**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Provider readiness remains uneven due to cost, technical complexity, and coordination challenges with vendors and health plans.
- **Specific request:** CMS should offer technical assistance, pilots, incentives, and public reporting of API usage metrics by provider type, plan, and geographic region.

**Topic 4: Drug Prior Authorization Inclusion**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Extending electronic PA to drugs across both benefits can reduce administrative burden and treatment delays, which are especially harmful for CF patients who require intensive lifelong therapies.
- **Specific request:** CMS should finalize drug inclusion and pair it with substantive reforms that ensure continuity of care and reduce unnecessary PA barriers.

**Topic 5: Detailed Denial Explanations**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Generic denial language does not give patients or providers enough information to correct missing documentation, resubmit, or appeal.
- **Specific request:** Denial notices should include specific clinical criteria or coverage policy, identify missing documentation, and provide clear next steps for resubmission or appeal; vague phrases such as failure to establish medical necessity should not suffice.

**Topic 6: Drug PA Timelines and Extensions**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support / Modify
- **Rationale:** Delays of even a few days can increase CF patients' risk of exacerbations, hospitalization, and irreversible lung damage.
- **Specific request:** CMS should require 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited drug PA decisions, further shorten timelines where feasible including considering 24 hours for all drug PA decisions, limit extensions, and require timely notice and clear justification for any extension.

**Topic 7: Alternative Funding Programs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Clarify / Modify
- **Rationale:** AFPs can place patients in a prior authorization standstill by refusing clear coverage determinations unless patients enroll in third-party programs, undermining appeal rights and procedural protections.
- **Specific request:** CMS should clarify that AFPs and similar utilization management or coverage-related requirements must comply with prior authorization standards, denial explanation requirements, appeal instructions, and enforceable timelines.

**Topic 8: Chronic Condition Reauthorization Protections**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** People with CF have stable lifelong diagnoses and often remain on the same indicated therapies indefinitely; repeated reauthorization adds burden with little clinical value.
- **Specific request:** CMS should adopt extended approval periods, approvals valid for the duration of treatment or clinically appropriate periods, and gold carding for providers with strong approval histories.

**Topic 9: Step Therapy and DME RFIs**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Step therapy and DME PA can create clinically inappropriate delays or force patients to retry ineffective/intolerable therapies or lose access to needed supplemental oxygen.
- **Specific request:** CMS should ensure plans honor prior step therapy history, use payer-to-payer APIs for continuity, and reduce unnecessary PA for DME such as liquid oxygen.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** The Foundation supports extending PA API requirements to drugs and emphasizes that technical implementation must translate into reduced delays for patients with complex medication needs.
- **S14:** The comment supports drug PA requirements across pharmacy benefits and stresses formulary/coverage transparency for prescription drugs.
- **S16:** The comment directly supports specific PA denial reasons but asks CMS to require detailed, actionable explanations with criteria, missing documentation, and appeal/resubmission steps.
- **S17:** The comment does not expressly request structured codes, but supports specificity sufficient for action and accountability.
- **S20:** The Foundation supports 24-hour expedited drug PA decisions and urges CMS to consider a 24-hour standard for all drug PA decisions where feasible.
- **S21:** The comment supports drug PA timelines but highlights adoption challenges and the need for technical assistance, pilots, and incentives.
- **S29:** The comment asks CMS to collect and publicly report API usage metrics including utilization rates by provider type, plan, and region.
- **S30:** The comment asks CMS to ensure accessible patient-facing interfaces and support for people with limited English proficiency, disabilities, or limited digital access.
- **S34:** The comment supports regular public reporting but does not specify exact frequency.
- **S35:** The comment supports public reporting of PA activity and outcomes, disaggregated by condition, service type, geography, and demographics.
- **S43:** The comment supports strong and aligned PA timelines and urges shorter timelines where feasible.
- **S66-S82:** The comment responds to RFIs on step therapy and lab/DME, urging CMS to protect continuity of care, honor prior step therapy history, and reduce unnecessary PA for items such as liquid oxygen.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize electronic prior authorization requirements for prescription drugs across medical and pharmacy benefits.
2. Make previously approved prior authorizations available through payer-to-payer APIs when patients switch payers.
3. Provide real-time prescription drug cost, coverage, and PA status information through the Patient Access API.
4. Establish usability and equity standards for patient-facing digital interfaces, language access, interpreter support, and non-digital access.
5. Provide technical assistance, pilots, and incentives for provider API and ePA adoption.
6. Publicly report API usage metrics by provider type, plan, and geographic region.
7. Require detailed actionable denial explanations that identify criteria, missing documentation, and resubmission/appeal steps.
8. Maintain 72-hour standard and 24-hour expedited drug PA timelines and consider 24-hour decisions for all drug PA requests.
9. Limit PA timeframe extensions and require timely notice and justification.
10. Clarify that alternative funding programs and similar arrangements must comply with PA determinations, denial notices, appeal rights, and timelines.
11. Reduce repeat prior authorizations for chronic conditions through extended approvals and gold carding.
12. Require public reporting of PA requests, approvals, denials, appeals, and extensions, disaggregated by condition, service type, geography, and demographics.
13. Require plans to honor prior step therapy history and use interoperability tools to prevent treatment disruptions.
14. Explore ways to reduce unnecessary DME prior authorizations, including for liquid oxygen.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** PA delays, repeated reauthorizations, vague denials, alternative funding program standstills, uneven provider API adoption, inequitable access to digital tools, and lack of public PA/API accountability.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** CF patients may face delayed treatment, infections, lung exacerbations, costly hospitalizations, irreversible lung damage, loss of appeal rights, and reduced ability to work or participate in daily life when DME is delayed.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Provider readiness gaps, cost, technical complexity, vendor and plan coordination, limited digital/broadband access, language barriers, timeframe extensions, and payer practices that avoid formal determinations.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Nearly 19% of prior authorization-related cases reported to the Foundation over the last 5 years involved patients being unaware PA had not been submitted; in 2023, 56% of Compass callers with PA or formulary issues experienced a delay in care; a WEDI survey found one third of providers had not begun API implementation and nearly two-thirds were unsure of progress.
- **Studies or research referenced:** CF Foundation Compass Case Management Data; WEDI Interoperability and Prior Authorization Survey Results (February 2026); Pasley et al., Pediatric Pulmonology 2025 on mental health of pediatric CF patients after elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor therapy.
- **Examples provided:** CF patients needing lifelong therapies, patients changing insurance and needing new PA, tolerability issues with Trikafta, step therapy forcing retries of intolerable treatments, and access barriers for liquid oxygen.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** People with cystic fibrosis, chronic disease patients, caregivers, providers, plans, API vendors, policymakers, researchers, and patient assistance/case management programs.
- **Economic implications:** Reduced repeat PA and delays could lower administrative burden, avoid costly hospitalizations, and allow clinical teams to focus resources on care rather than paperwork. Implementation may require investment in APIs, reporting, technical assistance, and accessible interfaces.
- **Technical feasibility:** The Foundation supports API-based approaches but notes readiness gaps and recommends assistance, pilots, and metrics to ensure adoption.
- **Patient care impact:** The comment identifies high potential patient benefit from faster decisions, continuity of care, fewer reauthorizations, clearer denial information, and reduced step therapy/DME delays.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with strong requests for additional patient protections.
- **Tone:** Professional, patient-centered, and urgent.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Prior authorization is a time-consuming process that can burden providers, divert valuable resources away from direct patient care, and cause delays in patient access to needed treatment." - Context: Framing the burden of PA for CF patients.
2. "We strongly support CMS's proposal to extend electronic prior authorization requirements to prescription drugs across both medical and pharmacy benefits." - Context: Core position on the proposed drug PA expansion.
3. "Explanations that rely on broad or non-specific language... do not provide sufficient information." - Context: Request for actionable denial explanations.
4. "Because CF is a progressive disease, patients who delay or forgo treatment - even for as little as a few days - face increased risk." - Context: Rationale for shorter and enforceable PA timelines.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - The comment supports faster PA deadlines, limits on extensions, and 24-hour expedited decisions.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - It discusses provider administrative burden, technical assistance needs, and costly hospitalizations from delayed care.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Repeated reauthorizations and PA paperwork are described as diverting provider resources from care.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - The Foundation asks CMS to address language access, disability access, interpreter support, and limited broadband/digital access.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - The comment cites provider readiness gaps and recommends assistance, pilots, incentives, and usage metrics.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Timely access to CF therapies, PA status, cost/coverage information, and DME is the core concern.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - The comment seeks clear PA status, cost/coverage information, detailed denial notices, and public PA reporting.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - It calls for coordination among CMS, providers, vendors, health plans, and patients to ensure API adoption and continuity.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The comment addresses real-world PA, reauthorization, step therapy, appeal, payer transition, and DME workflows.
